description: We are Kali users, a team of secondary school students who code for fun and love building projects together. We aren't professionals, but we are genuinely passionate about programming, exploring new tech, and tackling cool challenges. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we're bringing our enthusiasm to turn open data into a working project, level up our skills, and have a great time building together.
summary: Developed by **Team Kali Users** using HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and React, **Junior Astronaut: Moon Outpost** is an interactive educational web game designed to spark children's passion for space science by placing them in the role of a Mission Commander helping a stranded astronaut named Tobish survive and build a lunar city. Tailored to two age groups (7–9 and 10–12), the game integrates authentic data from official NASA portals (DONKI, MSL RAD, OSDR, Moon Trek, and NTRS) to simulate real solar flares and space weather across six progressive missions. Players manage five vital daily resources—oxygen, energy, radiation shielding, food, and communications—by visiting base modules to learn NASA science facts, answering trivia, making strategic trade-offs with clear outcomes, and playing physics-based mini-games like stacking regolith shields, jumping craters, accounting for a 1.3-second signal delay, and deflecting meteorites, ultimately turning complex astrophysics into an engaging, hands-on STEM experience.
details:
Junior Astronaut: Moon Outpost is an interactive educational web game designed to teach children about space exploration, lunar survival, and real-world astrophysics.

How It Works

The game begins with a short animated intro where a character named Tobish crash-lands on the Moon. Fortunately, his communications computer still works, allowing the player—acting as the Mission Commander—to guide him from Earth. After entering their name, launching the rocket, and selecting their age bracket (7–9 or 10–12 years old, which dynamically adjusts question difficulty), the player manages a lunar base across six progressive missions, evolving it from a basic garden into a full colony and eventually a lunar city.

Each in-game day follows a structured loop:

  1. Space Weather Briefing: Players review real historical solar flares and geomagnetic storms sourced from NASA's DONKI database, complete with authentic dates.
  2. Base Exploration & Resource Management: Players direct Tobish to five key modules—the Greenhouse, Solar Panels, Radiation Shelter, Communications Antenna, and Science Lab—to monitor and replenish five vital daily resources: oxygen, energy, radiation shielding, food, and communications. If any resource hits zero, the mission fails.
  3. NASA Fact Cards & Trivia: Interacting with each module reveals scientific facts backed by NASA data followed by a quiz question. Correct answers award resources that the player must strategically allocate.
  4. Dilemmas & Mini-Games: Players face critical trade-offs (e.g., routing limited power to life support versus scientific research) and see immediate feedback on both their choice and the alternative outcomes. Each mission also features an action-oriented mini-game: stacking lunar regolith blocks (Tetris-style) to build radiation shielding, driving a rover over craters, catching radio signals while compensating for the real 1.3-second Earth-Moon communication delay, and deflecting incoming meteorites.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • STEM Literacy & Critical Thinking: By turning resource management and trade-offs into core mechanics, children learn cause-and-effect reasoning, systems thinking, and basic space science without feeling like they are taking a test.
  • Real-World Data Engagement: Integrating actual NASA datasets (DONKI, MSL RAD, OSDR, Moon Trek, and NTRS) bridges the gap between classroom science and real space agency research, inspiring curiosity about careers in aerospace and STEM.
  • Constructive Failure: Rather than simply ending the game when resources run out, the failure screen explains the exact scientific reason the outpost failed and allows players to retry the mission with extra supplies, encouraging resilience and iterative learning.

Creativity & Design Considerations

  • Role-Reversal Storytelling: Making the child the "Mission Commander" talking to a stranded astronaut creates immediate emotional investment and agency, reinforced by interactive touches like pressing the launch button themselves.
  • Adaptive Accessibility: Splitting content into two age tiers ensures younger players aren't overwhelmed by complex jargon while older players remain challenged.
  • Authentic Physics as Gameplay: Instead of generic arcade challenges, mechanics like the 1.3-second signal delay mini-game and regolith radiation shielding directly translate real lunar engineering problems into intuitive play.
